## Today {.unnumbered}

Some numbers rest on a lot of data, some on very little. Today we learn the
Bayesian way of taking that into account, first with restaurants and a well,
then with lung cancer in Pennsylvania. Reading: **Moraga Ch. 3, 4 and
§5.1--5.3**.

::: {.callout-note}
## By the end of today you can

1. explain *prior*, *data* and *posterior* with an everyday example;
2. explain why the SIR of a small county is unreliable;
3. say what *shrinkage* does, and to which counties;
4. compute a 95% credible interval by hand, and read one off a posterior
   curve;
5. read a smoothed map, credible intervals and an exceedance map made with
   R-INLA.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-fold: false

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(SpatialEpi)   # pennLC
library(INLA)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Install INLA before class.** It is not on CRAN:

```r
install.packages("INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"))
```
:::

# The Bayesian idea in one example

## Two restaurants

| | Number of reviews | Average rating |
|---|---|---|
| Restaurant A | 2 | 5.0 ★ |
| Restaurant B | 800 | 4.7 ★ |

Which one would you pick? Most people pick B, even though A has the higher
average: two five-star reviews could come from the owner's friends. Without
noticing, you did three things.

1. You started from what you know about restaurants in general: a typical one
   gets about 4.0 stars. That is the **prior**.
2. You looked at each restaurant's own reviews. That is the **data**.
3. You combined the two, trusting the reviews more when there are many. That is
   the **posterior**, your best guess.

## The best guess is a weighted average

Say our prior is worth 10 reviews of 4.0 stars. The best guess for a
restaurant is

$$
\text{best guess} \;=\; w \times \text{its average} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 4.0,
\qquad w = \frac{\text{its reviews}}{\text{its reviews} + 10}.
$$

$w$ is how much we **trust its own reviews**, between 0 and 1. In R:

```{r}
#| label: restaurants

best_guess <- function(reviews, average, prior_mean = 4.0, prior_worth = 10) {
  w <- reviews / (reviews + prior_worth)        # trust in its own reviews
  w * average + (1 - w) * prior_mean            # weighted average
}

best_guess(reviews = 2,   average = 5.0)        # Restaurant A
best_guess(reviews = 800, average = 4.7)        # Restaurant B
```

Restaurant A's 5.0 is pulled back to `r round(best_guess(2, 5.0), 2)`: two
reviews are not enough to convince us. B barely moves, to
`r round(best_guess(800, 4.7), 2)`. Pulling an estimate toward the average is
called **shrinkage**.

## More reviews, less shrinkage

What if A kept getting five-star reviews?

```{r}
#| label: restaurants-more

tibble(reviews = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100, 800)) |>
  mutate(w          = round(reviews / (reviews + 10), 2),   # trust in its reviews
         best_guess = round(best_guess(reviews, 5.0), 2))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-restaurants
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Best guess for a restaurant whose reviews all give 5.0 stars, as reviews accumulate."

tibble(reviews = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(guess = best_guess(reviews, 5.0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(reviews, guess)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(4, 5), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = c(3.95, 5.05), hjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           label = c("prior: a typical restaurant (4.0)", "its own reviews (5.0)")) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(data = tibble(reviews = 2, guess = best_guess(2, 5.0)), size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.4, y = best_guess(2, 5.0), label = "Restaurant A",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of reviews (log scale)", y = "Best guess (stars)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

With 2 reviews, the guess stays close to the prior. With 10 reviews, as many as
the prior is worth, it sits exactly halfway. With hundreds, the prior hardly
matters.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the data. The more data,
the more the data win.
:::

# Learning one test at a time: is the well water safe?

## The story

A family tests its well for arsenic ten times. The EPA limit is 10 µg/L. Their
question: **how often is this water above the limit?** Call that share
$\theta$: $\theta = 0.2$ means unsafe one test in five.

```{r}
#| label: data-arsenic

epa   <- 10                                          # EPA limit, µg/L
conc  <- c(14, 7, 12, 18, 11, 15, 9, 13, 14, 14)     # 10 tests (illustrative)
above <- as.integer(conc > epa)                      # 1 = above, 0 = below
above
```

We do not start from nothing. In nearby wells, about **half** of past tests
were above the limit: 5 of 10. That is our **prior**, centred on
$\theta = 0.5$. A Beta curve keeps the score: Beta(5, 5) means 5 tests above
and 5 below, borrowed from the neighbours. Each new test above the limit adds 1
to the first number, each test below adds 1 to the second.

## Watching the posterior learn

In each panel, red dotted is what we believed **before** the test, green is
what we believe **after**.

```{r}
#| label: fn-update
#| code-fold: true

plot_update <- function(a, b, x, n, title = "") {
  theta <- seq(0, 1, 0.001)
  plot(theta, dbeta(theta, a, b), type = "l", lty = 3, lwd = 3, col = "red",
       ylim = c(0, 4), bty = "l", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "",
       main = title)                                            # before
  if (n > 0)                                                    # no test, no update
    lines(theta, dbeta(theta, a + x, b + n - x), lwd = 3, col = "darkgreen")  # after
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-seq-chain
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "Each panel starts from the previous panel's green curve and adds one test."

par(mfrow = c(3, 4), mar = c(4, 2, 2, 1))

a <- 5; b <- 5                                      # prior: 5 of 10 above in nearby wells
plot_update(a, b, 0, 0, title = "Before testing: nearby wells")

for (i in 1:10) {
  plot_update(a, b, above[i], 1,
              title = paste0("#", i, ": ", conc[i], " ug/L",
                             ifelse(above[i] == 1, " (above)", " (below)")))
  a <- a + above[i]                                 # after ...
  b <- b + 1 - above[i]                             # ... becomes next before
}
```

Three things to notice:

1. A test above the limit pushes the curve right; a test below pushes it left
   (tests 2 and 7).
2. The curve gets **taller and narrower**: more tests, more certainty.
3. Each panel's green curve becomes the next panel's red curve. That is
   Bayesian learning.

::: {.callout-note}
**Why does the y-axis stop at 4?** It shows a density, not a probability, so
it can exceed 1; the area under each curve is 1. We fix it at 4 so the panels
can be compared.
:::

## What do we know after ten tests?

```{r}
#| label: read-post

a / (a + b)                                      # best guess for θ
qbeta(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)                     # 95% credible interval
1 - pbeta(0.5, a, b)                             # P(unsafe more than half the time)
```

Our best guess is that the water is above the limit about
`r round(100 * a / (a + b))`% of the time, and with 95% probability between
`r round(100 * qbeta(0.025, a, b))`% and `r round(100 * qbeta(0.975, a, b))`%
(the **credible interval**). The probability that it is unsafe more than half
the time is `r sprintf("%.2f", 1 - pbeta(0.5, a, b))`. Bayesian results answer
the family's question directly, as a probability.

Where does `r round(100 * a / (a + b))`% come from? The well's own tests say
`r sum(above)` of 10, `r round(100 * mean(above))`%. The nearby wells say 50%.
The prior is worth 10 tests and the well has 10 of its own, so the answer sits
halfway. It is the restaurant formula again:

$$
`r sprintf("%.2f", a / (a + b))` \;=\; w \times `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(above))`
\;+\; (1 - w) \times 0.50,
\qquad w = \frac{10}{10 + 10} = 0.5.
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
We start from what we already know, here the nearby wells, and each new test
updates it. More data, a narrower curve, more certainty.
:::

# Counties: why small counties need help

## The data

We rebuild the Pennsylvania lung cancer counts from the SIR lecture: $O$
observed cases, $E$ expected cases, and SIR $= O/E$.

```{r}
#| label: recap
#| code-fold: true

data(pennLC)
d <- pennLC$data

ref <- d |>
  group_by(race, gender, age) |>
  summarise(r = sum(cases) / sum(population), .groups = "drop")   # reference rates

county <- d |>
  left_join(ref, by = c("race", "gender", "age")) |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(O = sum(cases), E = sum(population * r), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(county = as.character(county), SIR = O / E)

pa <- st_as_sf(pennLC$spatial.polygon) |>
  st_set_crs(4326) |>
  mutate(county = names(pennLC$spatial.polygon)) |>
  st_transform(5070) |>                                           # Albers
  left_join(county, by = "county")

sir_breaks <- c(0, 0.67, 0.83, 0.95, 1.05, 1.2, 1.5, Inf)
sir_fill   <- scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, drop = FALSE, name = "Risk")
```

## The SIR map

```{r}
#| label: fig-sir
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Lung cancer SIRs, Pennsylvania counties."

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  sir_fill +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

Which counties have the most extreme SIRs?

```{r}
#| label: sir-extremes

extremes <- county |>
  arrange(SIR) |>
  slice(c(1:3, 65:67)) |>                           # 3 lowest, 3 highest
  mutate(E = round(E, 1), SIR = round(SIR, 2))
extremes
```

Of these six counties, `r sum(extremes$E < 20)` expect fewer than 20 cases;
the median county expects `r round(median(county$E))`. A few cases more or less
move their SIR a lot. Small counties are like restaurants with two reviews.

## One more case

How fragile is a small county's SIR? Here is what **a single extra case** would
do, in the three smallest and the three largest counties:

```{r}
#| label: one-more-case

one_more <- county |>
  arrange(E) |>
  slice(c(1:3, 65:67)) |>                           # 3 smallest, 3 largest
  mutate(SIR_one_more = (O + 1) / E)                # with one more case

one_more |>
  mutate(E = round(E, 1), SIR = round(SIR, 2), SIR_one_more = round(SIR_one_more, 2))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
tc   <- function(x) sub("Mck", "McK", tools::toTitleCase(x))   # county names
f2   <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
om   <- function(name, col) one_more[[col]][one_more$county == name]
flip <- tc(one_more$county[cut(one_more$SIR, sir_breaks) !=
                           cut(one_more$SIR_one_more, sir_breaks)])
```

One more case would move Forest's SIR from `r f2(om("forest", "SIR"))` to
`r f2(om("forest", "SIR_one_more"))`, and Cameron's from
`r f2(om("cameron", "SIR"))` to `r f2(om("cameron", "SIR_one_more"))`.
`r if (length(flip) > 0) paste0(paste(flip, collapse = " and "), " would even change colour on the map. ") else ""`Philadelphia's
SIR would not move at two decimals. On the map, the colour of a small county
can hinge on a single person.

## The funnel plot

How far can an SIR stray by chance alone? If a county's true risk were exactly
the state's, its SIR would still fall, about 95% of the time, within
$1 \pm 1.96/\sqrt{E}$. Plotted against $E$, that range is a funnel.

```{r}
#| label: fig-funnel
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "SIRs against expected cases. Grey: where about 95% of SIRs fall by chance alone."

funnel <- tibble(E = exp(seq(log(4), log(1500), length.out = 200))) |>
  mutate(lo = 1 - 1.96 / sqrt(E),                   # chance range of the SIR
         hi = 1 + 1.96 / sqrt(E))

labelled <- filter(county, county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "juniata", "philadelphia"))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = funnel, aes(E, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = county, aes(E, SIR)) +
  geom_text(data = labelled, aes(E, SIR, label = tools::toTitleCase(county)),
            nudge_y = 0.07, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Expected cases (log scale)", y = "SIR") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The funnel is wide on the left. Potter's 1.37 and Sullivan's 0.40 sit inside
it: they could be chance. Philadelphia's 1.16 is far outside: with more than
1,200 expected cases, a 16% excess is not chance.

::: {.callout-important}
## The problem in one sentence
A raw SIR mixes real differences in risk with chance, and chance is largest in
small counties.
:::

# Shrinkage: the restaurant formula for counties

## Same formula, new names

| Restaurants | Counties |
|---|---|
| number of reviews | expected cases $E$ |
| its average rating | its SIR |
| a typical restaurant, 4.0 | the state average, 1 |
| prior worth 10 reviews | state average worth $k$ expected cases |
| trust in its own reviews, $w$ | trust in its own SIR, $w$ |

So each county gets

$$
\text{estimate} \;=\; w \times \text{SIR} \;+\; (1 - w) \times 1,
\qquad w = \frac{E}{E + k}.
$$

A big county (large $E$) keeps its SIR. A small county borrows from the state.

## Who decides $k$? The data

For the restaurants we picked 10 ourselves. For counties, R estimates $k$ from
the 67 SIRs:

- if counties differ **much more** than chance alone would produce, real
  differences are large, the state average is worth little, and $k$ is small;
- if counties differ **about as much** as chance would produce, the state
  average is worth a lot, and $k$ is large.

Letting the data choose the prior this way is called **empirical Bayes**
(Clayton and Kaldor 1987; Marshall 1991). `EBest()` in **spdep** does it in
one line.

```{r}
#| label: eb-global

eb <- EBest(pa$O, pa$E)                              # cases, expected cases
pa$RR_eb <- eb$estmm                                 # shrunk estimate

k <- with(attr(eb, "parameters"), b / a)             # state worth k expected cases
k
pa$w <- pa$E / (pa$E + k)                            # trust in own SIR
```

The state average is worth about `r round(k)` expected cases. Here are five
counties, from small to large:

```{r}
#| label: eb-table

pa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "venango", "lehigh", "philadelphia")) |>
  arrange(E) |>
  transmute(county, E = round(E), SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            w = round(w, 2), estimate = round(RR_eb, 2))
```

Sullivan expects 7 cases against the state's `r round(k)`: we trust its SIR
only `r round(100 * pa$w[pa$county == "sullivan"])`%, and its estimate is
almost the state's. Philadelphia, with more than 1,200 expected cases, keeps
`r round(100 * pa$w[pa$county == "philadelphia"])`% of its SIR. Potter and
Venango have the same SIR, 1.37, like two restaurants with the same average,
but Venango rests on three times more cases, so it stays higher:
`r sprintf("%.2f", pa$RR_eb[pa$county == "venango"])` against
`r sprintf("%.2f", pa$RR_eb[pa$county == "potter"])`.

## Where do we borrow?

```{r}
#| label: fig-weights
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Trust in each county's own SIR. Dark: we keep the county's SIR. Light: we borrow from the state."

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = w), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Purples", direction = 1, limits = c(0, 1),
                       name = "Trust w") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

The map of $w$ is a map of population: the rural north and centre borrow the
most, the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas the least.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
Small counties borrow from the state; big counties keep their own SIR. The
data decide how much to borrow.
:::

## From one number to a whole curve

Empirical Bayes gives one number per county, but behind it is a whole curve, as
for the well. The state average, worth $k \approx$ `r round(k)` expected cases,
is the **prior**: a curve centred on 1 (red, dotted). The county's own $O$
cases for $E$ expected are the **data** (blue). The **posterior** combines the
two (green). Its centre, the **best guess**, is the empirical Bayes estimate,
$(k + O)/(k + E)$. The middle 95% of its area, shaded, is the **95% credible
interval**: the county's true risk lies in it with 95% probability.

```{r}
#| label: three-counties

three <- county |>
  filter(county %in% c("sullivan", "potter", "philadelphia")) |>
  mutate(w          = E / (E + k),                      # trust in own SIR
         best_guess = (k + O) / (k + E),                # = empirical Bayes
         CI_low     = qgamma(0.025, k + O, k + E),      # 95% credible interval
         CI_high    = qgamma(0.975, k + O, k + E)) |>
  arrange(E)

three |>
  mutate(across(c(E, SIR, w, best_guess, CI_low, CI_high), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-prior-data-posterior
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Prior (red), data (blue) and posterior (green) for a small, a middle and a large county. Shaded: the 95% credible interval. Dashed: the best guess."

curves <- function(name) {
  x <- filter(three, county == name)
  tibble(theta     = seq(0.01, 2.5, by = 0.002),
         Prior     = dgamma(theta, k, k),                # state, worth k cases
         Data      = dgamma(theta, x$O + 1, x$E),        # own cases only
         Posterior = dgamma(theta, k + x$O, k + x$E),    # both together
         county    = tools::toTitleCase(name))
}

cur <- bind_rows(lapply(three$county, curves)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Prior, Data, Posterior), names_to = "curve", values_to = "density") |>
  mutate(curve  = factor(curve, c("Prior", "Data", "Posterior")),
         county = factor(county, tools::toTitleCase(three$county)))    # small to large
lines <- mutate(three, county = factor(tools::toTitleCase(county), levels(cur$county)))
shade <- cur |>
  filter(curve == "Posterior") |>
  left_join(select(lines, county, CI_low, CI_high), by = "county") |>
  filter(theta >= CI_low, theta <= CI_high)                          # middle 95%

ggplot(cur, aes(theta, density)) +
  geom_area(data = shade, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(data = lines, aes(xintercept = best_guess), colour = "darkgreen",
             linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = curve, linetype = curve), linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ county, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Prior = "red", Data = "blue", Posterior = "darkgreen")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Prior = 3, Data = 1, Posterior = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk", y = NULL, colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
th <- function(name, col) three[[col]][three$county == name]
```

Sullivan's green curve lies almost on the red prior: its `r th("sullivan", "O")`
cases cannot outweigh `r round(k)` borrowed ones, and its interval,
`r f2(th("sullivan", "CI_low"))` to `r f2(th("sullivan", "CI_high"))`, is about
as wide as the prior itself. Potter's SIR of `r f2(th("potter", "SIR"))` is
pulled back to `r f2(th("potter", "best_guess"))`, and its interval,
`r f2(th("potter", "CI_low"))` to `r f2(th("potter", "CI_high"))`, contains 1:
we cannot say that Potter's risk is above the state's. Philadelphia's curve lies
on its own data, and its narrow interval,
`r f2(th("philadelphia", "CI_low"))` to `r f2(th("philadelphia", "CI_high"))`,
lies entirely above 1.

## The credible interval by hand

The posterior curve above is set by two numbers:

$$
a = k + O \;\;\text{(borrowed + own cases)}, \qquad
b = k + E \;\;\text{(borrowed + own expected cases)}.
$$

With a calculator, four steps give the 95% credible interval:

| Step | Formula |
|---|---|
| 1. best guess | $a / b$ |
| 2. spread (standard deviation) | $\sqrt{a} \,/\, b$ |
| 3. low end | best guess $- \, 1.96 \times$ spread |
| 4. high end | best guess $+ \, 1.96 \times$ spread |

This is the familiar "estimate $\pm$ 1.96 standard errors", applied to the
posterior. R's `qgamma()` instead cuts exactly 2.5% of the area off each side
of the curve. Both, for Sullivan:

```{r}
#| label: by-hand

su     <- filter(county, county == "sullivan")
a      <- k + su$O                                  # borrowed + own cases
b      <- k + su$E                                  # borrowed + own expected
best   <- a / b                                     # step 1
spread <- sqrt(a) / b                               # step 2
round(c(a = a, b = b, best_guess = best, spread = spread), 3)

round(best + c(-1.96, 1.96) * spread, 2)            # steps 3-4: by hand
round(qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b), 2)             # exact: cut 2.5% each side
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-by-hand
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Sullivan's posterior. Grey: the 2.5% cut off on each side. Green: the middle 95%, the exact credible interval. Black bar: the interval by hand."

ex   <- qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), a, b)               # exact interval
hand <- best + c(-1.96, 1.96) * spread              # by hand
d    <- tibble(x = seq(best - 5 * spread, best + 5 * spread, length.out = 600),
               y = dgamma(x, a, b))
top  <- max(d$y)

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x <= ex[1]), fill = "grey70") +                 # lower 2.5%
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x >= ex[2]), fill = "grey70") +                 # upper 2.5%
  geom_area(data = filter(d, x >= ex[1], x <= ex[2]), fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best, colour = "darkgreen", linetype = 2) +         # best guess
  annotate("text", x = c(ex[1] - 0.6 * spread, best + 0.9 * spread, ex[2] + 0.6 * spread),
           y = top * c(0.12, 0.45, 0.12), label = c("2.5%", "95%", "2.5%")) +
  annotate("segment", x = hand[1], xend = hand[2], y = -0.12 * top,
           yend = -0.12 * top, linewidth = 1.2) +                            # by hand
  annotate("text", x = best, y = -0.22 * top, size = 3.5,
           label = "by hand: best guess +/- 1.96 x spread") +
  labs(x = "Relative risk, Sullivan County", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

Here $a$ is large, about `r round(a)`, so the curve is almost symmetric and the
two intervals agree to about 0.01. When a county borrows little, the curve is
lopsided and the interval by hand is only an approximation; you will see this
in Exercise 7.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
A credible interval is read off the posterior curve: cut 2.5% of the area on
each side. By hand, best guess $\pm$ 1.96 $\times$ spread comes close.
:::

# Full Bayes with R-INLA

Empirical Bayes gives one number per county. A **full Bayesian** model does the
same shrinkage but returns a whole posterior curve per county, like the green
curves of the well. That tells us **how sure** we are. INLA is a fast way to
fit such models (Moraga Ch. 3--4).

We use the **BYM2** model (Moraga §5.3). Instead of borrowing from the whole
state, each county borrows mostly from its **neighbours**, the way the family
borrowed from nearby wells. We use the queen neighbours from the Moran's I
lecture.

```{r}
#| label: fig-inla-diagram
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "What goes into INLA, and what comes out."

box <- tibble(
  x     = c(0, 0, 0, 2.7, 5.1, 7.6, 7.6),
  y     = c(2, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1.6, 0.4),
  w     = c(2.3, 2.3, 2.3, 1.1, 2.3, 2.0, 2.0),
  fill  = c(rep("#DCE9F5", 3), "#F4CCCC", "#D9EAD3", "#D9EAD3", "#D9EAD3"),
  label = c("The county's\nown cases", "Its neighbours'\ncases",
            "How different the\n67 counties are", "INLA",
            "One posterior curve\nper county", "Best guess",
            "95% credible\ninterval"))
arr <- tibble(x    = c(1.15, 1.15, 1.15, 3.25, 6.25, 6.25),
              y    = c(2, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1),
              xend = c(2.15, 2.15, 2.15, 3.95, 6.6, 6.6),
              yend = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1.6, 0.4))

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = arr, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey40",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_tile(data = box, aes(x, y, width = w, height = 0.75, fill = fill), colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = box, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  theme_void()
```

How to read the `inla()` call below:

| Piece of the code | In words |
|---|---|
| `O ~ 1` | model the observed cases around one overall level of risk |
| `f(id, model = "bym2", graph = g)` | each county gets its own risk, pulled toward its neighbours (listed in `g`) |
| `family = "poisson", E = E` | cases are counts, compared with expected cases, so results read like an SIR |
| `control...` | only asks INLA to keep the results we need |

```{r}
#| label: m2

dat <- st_drop_geometry(pa) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())                          # one index per county

nb <- poly2nb(pa, queen = TRUE)                      # queen neighbours
nb2INLA("pa.adj", nb)                                # write for INLA
g  <- inla.read.graph("pa.adj")

m2 <- inla(O ~ 1 + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = g),
           family = "poisson", E = E, data = dat,
           control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
           control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE))

dat$RR_bym2 <- m2$summary.fitted.values$mean         # posterior mean risk
dat$LL <- m2$summary.fitted.values$`0.025quant`      # 95% credible interval, low
dat$UL <- m2$summary.fitted.values$`0.975quant`      # 95% credible interval, high
```

Read the formula as: log-risk = an overall level + a bump for each county that
borrows from its neighbours (Moraga §4.1).

## Three maps

```{r}
#| label: fig-maps
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Raw SIR, empirical Bayes and BYM2. Same colours."

pa |>
  select(county) |>
  left_join(select(dat, county, SIR, RR_eb, RR_bym2), by = "county") |>
  pivot_longer(c(SIR, RR_eb, RR_bym2), names_to = "estimate", values_to = "risk") |>
  mutate(estimate = factor(estimate, c("SIR", "RR_eb", "RR_bym2"),
                           c("SIR (raw)", "Empirical Bayes", "BYM2 (INLA)"))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(risk, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ estimate) +
  sir_fill +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The extreme colours of the raw map, mostly small rural counties, fade. What
remains is the broad pattern.

## Two counties, same SIR

Greene and Philadelphia have almost the same SIR. Here are INLA's posterior
curves for both, on the same horizontal axis. Green shaded: the 95% credible
interval. Green dashed: the best guess. Black: the state average, 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-two-curves
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "INLA's posterior curves for Greene and Philadelphia."

post_curve <- function(name) {
  i  <- which(dat$county == name)
  cv <- inla.smarginal(m2$marginals.fitted.values[[i]])   # INLA's curve
  data.frame(county = paste0(tools::toTitleCase(name), ": SIR = ", sprintf("%.2f", dat$SIR[i]),
                             ", E = ", round(dat$E[i])),
             x = cv$x, y = cv$y, RR = dat$RR_bym2[i], LL = dat$LL[i], UL = dat$UL[i])
}

cur2 <- bind_rows(post_curve("greene"), post_curve("philadelphia"))

ggplot(cur2, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(cur2, x >= LL, x <= UL), fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = RR), colour = "darkgreen", linetype = 2) +   # best guess
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1) +                                           # state average
  geom_line(colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ county, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Relative risk", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: two-counties

dat |>
  filter(county %in% c("greene", "philadelphia")) |>
  transmute(county, O, E = round(E), SIR = round(SIR, 2),
            RR_bym2 = round(RR_bym2, 2), LL = round(LL, 2), UL = round(UL, 2))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
dv <- function(name, col) dat[[col]][dat$county == name]
```

Greene's SIR rests on `r round(dv("greene", "E"))` expected cases: its curve
is wide, and its interval, `r f2(dv("greene", "LL"))` to
`r f2(dv("greene", "UL"))`, contains 1. Philadelphia's rests on
`r format(round(dv("philadelphia", "E")), big.mark = ",")`: its curve is narrow,
and its interval, `r f2(dv("philadelphia", "LL"))` to
`r f2(dv("philadelphia", "UL"))`, lies entirely above 1. Same SIR, very
different certainty.

## All 67 counties at once

Each row is one county's posterior curve seen from above: the bar is its 95%
credible interval, the dot its best guess, and the × its raw SIR. Small
counties are at the top. Red: the whole interval is above 1. Blue: the whole
interval is below 1. Grey: the interval contains 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-all-intervals
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "95% credible intervals (BYM2) for all 67 counties, smallest at the top."

ci_cols <- c("Entire interval above 1" = "#B2182B",
             "Interval contains 1"     = "grey55",
             "Entire interval below 1" = "#2166AC")

dat <- dat |>
  mutate(ci_class = factor(case_when(LL > 1 ~ names(ci_cols)[1],
                                     UL < 1 ~ names(ci_cols)[3],
                                     TRUE   ~ names(ci_cols)[2]), names(ci_cols)))

dat |>
  mutate(label = reorder(paste0(tc(county), " (E = ", round(E), ")"), -E)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +                               # state average
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = LL, xmax = UL, colour = ci_class), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = RR_bym2, colour = ci_class), size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = SIR, shape = "Raw SIR"), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = ci_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Raw SIR" = 4), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Relative risk", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical")
```

The same colours on the map:

```{r}
#| label: fig-ci-map
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Is each county's 95% credible interval above or below the state average?"

pa$ci_class <- dat$ci_class                          # same order as pa

ggplot(pa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ci_class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ci_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
mover <- dat |> mutate(move = abs(RR_bym2 - SIR)) |> slice_max(move, n = 1)
hi_ci <- tc(dat$county[dat$LL > 1])
lo_ci <- tc(dat$county[dat$UL < 1])
```

Small counties, at the top of the plot, have the longest bars, and their dots
sit far from their ×: `r tc(mover$county)`'s SIR of `r f2(mover$SIR)` becomes
`r f2(mover$RR_bym2)`. Only `r length(hi_ci)` counties have their whole interval
above 1 (`r paste(hi_ci, collapse = ", ")`), and `r length(lo_ci)` have it
below 1 (`r paste(lo_ci, collapse = ", ")`). For lung cancer, most counties are
indistinguishable from the state average.

## Borrowing from the neighbours

Empirical Bayes pulls every county toward the **state** average. BYM2 pulls it
mostly toward its **neighbours**. Potter, outlined in black, and its
neighbours:

```{r}
#| label: fig-potter
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Left: raw SIRs of Potter and its neighbours. Right: where each method puts Potter; the green bar is its 95% credible interval."

i    <- which(dat$county == "potter")
hood <- pa[c(i, nb[[i]]), ]                          # Potter, then its neighbours

p_map <- ggplot(hood) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = hood[1, ], fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +   # Potter
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = paste0(tc(county), "\n", sprintf("%.2f", SIR))),
               size = 3) +
  sir_fill +
  labs(title = "Raw SIRs") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

rows <- c("Neighbours' SIRs", "State average", "Potter, raw SIR",
          "Potter, empirical Bayes", "Potter, BYM2 best guess")
pts <- tibble(what  = factor(c(rep(rows[1], nrow(hood) - 1), rows[2:5]), rev(rows)),
              value = c(hood$SIR[-1], 1, dat$SIR[i], dat$RR_eb[i], dat$RR_bym2[i]))
bar <- tibble(what = factor(rows[5], rev(rows)), lo = dat$LL[i], hi = dat$UL[i])

p_line <- ggplot(pts, aes(value, what, colour = what)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_linerange(data = bar, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, y = what), inherit.aes = FALSE,
                 colour = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.2) +                    # credible interval
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "black", "blue", "purple", "darkgreen"),
                      breaks = rows, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Where does Potter land?", x = "Relative risk", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_map + p_line
```

```{r}
#| include: false
pot_nb <- dat[nb[[i]], ]
low_nb <- pot_nb |> filter(SIR < 1)
```

Empirical Bayes pulls Potter from `r f2(dv("potter", "SIR"))` to
`r f2(dv("potter", "RR_eb"))`, toward the state average. BYM2 puts it at
`r f2(dv("potter", "RR_bym2"))`, closer to its neighbours:
`r nrow(low_nb)` of its `r nrow(pot_nb)` neighbours
(`r paste0(tc(low_nb$county), " ", f2(low_nb$SIR), collapse = ", ")`) have SIRs
below 1. Cameron's SIR is high, `r f2(dv("cameron", "SIR"))`, but it rests on
only `r round(dv("cameron", "E"))` expected cases, so it counts for little.

## How sure are we? The exceedance map

For the well we asked: how likely is it that the water is unsafe more than half
the time? For each county we ask: how likely is it that its risk is above the
state average, $P(\theta > 1)$? This is the **exceedance probability**: the
area of the posterior curve to the right of 1. A county whose whole 95%
credible interval is above 1 has $P(\theta > 1) > 0.975$.

```{r}
#| label: exceed

dat$p_exc <- sapply(m2$marginals.fitted.values,
                    function(m) 1 - inla.pmarginal(1, m))   # P(θ > 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-exceed
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Probability that each county's lung cancer risk exceeds the state average (BYM2)."

exc_cols <- c("Probably lower (< 0.2)"  = "#2c7bb6",
              "Uncertain (0.2–0.8)"     = "grey90",
              "Probably higher (> 0.8)" = "#d7191c")

pa |>
  select(county) |>
  left_join(select(dat, county, p_exc), by = "county") |>
  mutate(exc = cut(p_exc, c(0, 0.2, 0.8, 1), labels = names(exc_cols),
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = exc), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = exc_cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)
```

Counties probably above average:
`r paste(tools::toTitleCase(dat$county[dat$p_exc > 0.8]), collapse = ", ")`.
Potter, despite its SIR of 1.37, is not among them
($P = `r sprintf("%.2f", dat$p_exc[dat$county == "potter"])`$): 22 cases are
not enough.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key idea
INLA does the same shrinkage, borrows from the neighbours, and tells us how
sure we are about each county.
:::

# In-class exercise {.unnumbered}

Work in pairs, 20 minutes.

1. **Restaurants.** Run `best_guess(2, 5.0, prior_worth = 100)`. What happens
   to A's best guess? And to B's, `best_guess(800, 4.7, prior_worth = 100)`?
   Why?
2. **Well water.** Suppose the family knew nothing about nearby wells and
   started from a flat prior, `a <- 1; b <- 1`. Rerun the updating. How does
   the final best guess change, and why?
3. **Funnel.** Cameron County has an SIR of
   `r sprintf("%.2f", county$SIR[county$county == "cameron"])` with only
   `r round(county$E[county$county == "cameron"])` expected cases. Is it inside
   the funnel? What is its empirical Bayes estimate,
   `pa$RR_eb[pa$county == "cameron"]`? Explain the difference.
4. **By hand.** Potter has $O$ = 22 cases for $E$ = 16.0 expected. With
   $k$ = 108, compute with a calculator $a$, $b$, the best guess, the spread
   and the 95% credible interval by hand. Check with
   `qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), 108 + 22, 108 + 16.0)`.
5. **Interpretation.** In two sentences for a county health officer, explain
   why Potter is not flagged even though its SIR is 1.37. Use its credible
   interval.

# Key takeaways {.unnumbered}

1. The posterior is a compromise between the prior and the data; the more
   data, the more the data win.
2. A raw SIR mixes real differences and chance; chance is largest in small
   counties.
3. Shrinkage: small counties borrow from the state (or their neighbours), big
   counties keep their SIR.
4. A posterior is a curve: its centre is the best guess, its middle 95% the
   credible interval. By hand: best guess $\pm$ 1.96 $\times$ spread.
5. Report how sure we are, not only the estimate: a county is clearly above
   average only when its whole credible interval is above 1.

# Words to know {.unnumbered}

| Word | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Prior | what we believe before seeing the data |
| Likelihood | what the data say |
| Posterior | what we believe after seeing the data |
| Best guess | the centre (mean) of the posterior curve |
| Spread | the standard deviation of the posterior curve |
| Credible interval | a range that contains the true value with 95% probability |
| Shrinkage | pulling unreliable estimates toward an average |
| Empirical Bayes | shrinkage where the data decide how much to shrink |
| Exceedance probability | the probability that a risk is above a threshold, e.g. the state average |

Bayes estimators. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C
(Applied Statistics)*, 40(2), 283--294.
